newsitem.title: BOSNIA: U.S. money guru urges currency board for Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: U.S. money guru urges currency board for Bosnia.

text.p: Bosnia's new currency will be superior to all other currencies in the Balkans provided a strict money policy is applied, and the government introduces other key reforms, a U.S. money expert has predicted.
A peacetime government first needs to set up a central bank operating under strict currency board rules and the time to act is now, Steve Hanke told reporters in Sarajevo last week.

Hanke said the system, with its emphasis on foreign reserve backing, would make the currency far more stable than the money now circulating in Bosnia from neighboring Croatia and Yugoslavia in addition to Bosnian dinars.
"The new money will be of equivalent quality to (German) marks," he said. "The new Bosnian currency will be the premier currency in the Balkans, period. That's the end of the story."

Hanke, a professor of applied economics who helped revive Argentina's peso and reform currencies in Estonia and Lithuania, came to Sarajevo to urge Bosnia to form its currency board as soon as possible.
"This is the issue. There is no other issue right now," Hanke said at a seminar last Friday.
Under the terms of the Dayton peace agreement, Bosnia is to have a single currency and a central bank which would operate currency board mechanisms for the initial six years.
The currency board method requires a full foreign reserve backing of the local currency and a fixed exchange rate against the reserve currency, which will probably be German marks, Hanke said.
But one year after the peace treaty was signed, the currency board has yet to start operating.
Most of the $1.8 billion pledged in foreign donations for the country's reconstruction are being held up until the central bank begins its work, Hanke said.
Launching the currency board was also a crucial test of Bosnia's fragile peace process, he said. "If it's not set up, the Dayton (peace accord) is finished, gone."
Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation and Serb republic officials are engaged in a battle over several central bank-related issues including the design of the new currency.
Serb officials have sent out mixed signals about their support for a single currency but diplomats say they are gradually coming round to the idea.
An IMF-appointed foreign governor of the central bank, Frenchman Serge Robert, is in place and three Bosnian members have been appointed to its governing board.
"Once you install the (currency) board, you'll have the foreign donations coming and it makes your balance of payments more favourable because you're getting capital inflow," Hanke said.
Some Serb officials have called for a separate currency in Serb territory but Hanke said they were "dreaming" because any alternative currency would lack foreign reserve backing.
"The currency board and Bosnia-Herzegovina money would drive this third rate currency out," he said.
Although he said that by installing the currency board method investors' foreign exchange risk would be eliminated, he doubted it would spark a wave of foreign investment in the war- torn country.
"The currency board gives you stability but you have to do all the other reforms and make the country literally, physically safe, so that it is attractive to foreign investors."
